title_en: Researchers are closer than ever to an AI-guided device to treat memory loss
summary: تیم تحقیقاتی دانشگاه پنسلوانیا با سیستم هوشمند SNS موفق به دریافت تاییدیه دستگاه پیشرو از سازمان FDA شد.

آزمایش‌های بالینی این فناوری مدرن برای سال ۲۰۲۷ برنامه‌ریزی شده است.
full_text: Researchers are closer than ever to an AI-guided device to treat memory loss In the late 1990s, a young Michael Kahana—then developing computer models of human memory—was invited to Harvard Medical School by a neurosurgeon friend to give grand rounds to the neurosurgery and neurology faculty. Afterward, he toured the ninth floor of Boston Children's Hospital. "It was the most important professional moment of my life," says Kahana, Edmund J. and Louise W. Kahn Term Professor of Psychology in the School of Arts & Sciences. On the ninth floor, patients with drug-resistant epilepsy were undergoing week-long monitoring with implanted electrodes to help plan a potentially curative surgery. Kahana observed a teen patient playing a video game as a recording system captured reams of never-analyzed data. Except for a small snippet used for seizure mapping, the data were deleted each night; there was nowhere to store such a massive amount of information. These were the roots of a decades-long adventure, as Kahana calls it, leading to the realization that it's possible to predict when somebody will remember and when somebody will forget. That journey took another step this past March when the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) bestowed a "breakthrough device designation" on the Smart Neurostimulation System (SNS), an implantable therapy created by Kahana and colleagues through their Penn spinout, Nia Therapeutics. The designation, which the FDA reserves for technologies that address unmet needs in serious conditions, qualifies the device for priority review, meaning it will likely be reviewed faster. Nia's SNS is the first device to receive the designation for TBI-related memory loss. The company, Kahana says, is preparing to begin clinical trials in 2027. The differentiator, he adds, is how the SNS employs artificial intelligence to guide a closed-loop technology, which analyzes distributed patterns of brain activity and uses personalized models to deliver bursts of stimulation during predicted memory lapses. "Sometimes I talk to people about this technology and they think that it's science fiction," says Daniel Rizzuto, who studied under Kahana and co-founded Nia Therapeutics with him. "It sounds like science fiction. But Mike and I have moved this technology from science fiction into science fact. And we've published multiple peer-reviewed papers showing our ability to improve human verbal memory using this personalized approach." A path to major advances Computational approaches to neural data, by Kahana and others, expanded with the rise of machine-learning methods that can understand how complex patterns of neural features predict behavioral measurements. Kahana has been publishing about those patterns for years. "Our Eureka! moment was when we realized that this huge amount of variation in the effects of stimulation could be explained," Kahana says. "A lot of it could be explained by the state of the brain when you stimulate." He and Rizzuto, for instance, teamed up at Penn in 2014 to launch the Restoring Active Memory project. The large-scale research allowed Kahana to explore how brain stimulation can modulate memory. Scaling the science to that level required Kahana and Rizzuto's team to set up testing sites at nine hospitals across the United States. One key insight from those studies: Once machine-learning pattern matching determines when someone is in a good or poor memory state, stimulation to the lateral temporal cortex—just over the person's left ear—can change the equation. The networks supporting memory are distributed across many brain regions and require technology that can listen to signals in multiple deep brain structures. That's where they place the 64 contacts in the Smart Neurostimulation System. When it senses the brain in a state that requires intervention, it delivers a burst of stimulation optimized to each patient's memory network. The results have been promising. Through a peer-reviewed study published in January 2023, for example, Kahana and Rizzuto reported that their device could boost memory by approximately 19% in patients with a history of moderate to severe traumatic brain injuries. In a subsequent 2024 publication, they showed they could boost memory by 28% in patients with epilepsy who had electrodes implanted near white matter tracts. This degree of improvement exceeds the usual benchmark physicians use for judging a clinically significant improvement. "For some of our patients, the closed-loop stimulation protocol improved their memory by the same amount that we would have expected their memory to have declined due to their brain injury," Rizzuto says. Kahana has trouble hiding his excitement. "The brain," he says, "is the last frontier, really. Right?" He is ambitious. Years of studies have helped, yet the pool of patients with implanted electrodes who can be observed is small. "If there are 27 million Americans who suffer from significant disability due to memory loss," Kahana says, "and if, of those 27 million Americans, 1% had a device that recorded brain data all the time...." It could open many doors. He doesn't say it, but it's implied in his pause. "This device not only includes a therapy, but it's also a data collection system for the human brain that will store vastly more neural data than I was able to collect in decades of research in neurosurgical patients," he adds. "These data could lead to unimaginable scientific and therapeutic advances."

title_en: University of Warwick and Monash University Researchers Identify Bacterial Molecule That Disarms Deadly Fungal Pathogen
summary: دانشمندان کشف کردند آنتی‌بیوتیک گلادیولین بدون کشتن قارچ کندیدا آلبیکنس، آن را غیرفعال می‌کند.

این روش مانع از ایجاد مقاومت دارویی در بیماران با سیستم ایمنی ضعیف می‌شود.
full_text: (IN BRIEF) Researchers from the University of Warwick and Monash University have discovered that gladiolin, a bacterial antibiotic, may help control dangerous fungal infections caused by Candida albicans by disarming the pathogen rather than killing it directly. The study, published in Current Biology, shows that gladiolin changes the fungus’s metabolism, causing it to burn through glucose more quickly and forcing it to switch from its invasive thread-like hyphae form back into a less harmful yeast state. This is significant because Candida albicans can become dangerous in critically ill or immunocompromised patients and on medical devices such as catheters, where it can invade tissue and form drug-resistant biofilms. The findings build on the team’s earlier work showing that gladiolin can also boost the effectiveness of amphotericin B, suggesting the molecule could help existing antifungal drugs work better while reducing the aggressive behaviour that makes fungal infections difficult to treat. (PRESS RELEASE) COVENTRY, 21-Aug-2026 — /EuropaWire/ — Researchers from the University of Warwick and Monash University have discovered a potential new way to stop one of the world’s most dangerous fungal pathogens, not by killing it directly, but by forcing it out of its aggressive infection mode. The study shows that gladiolin, a bacterial antibiotic, can disarm Candida albicans, one of the leading causes of life-threatening fungal infections, by pushing it back into a less harmful state. Fungal infections are estimated to kill around two million people worldwide every year, while treatment options remain limited and no vaccines are currently available. The findings have been published in Current Biology and are the latest outcome from the Monash Warwick Alliance’s antimicrobial resistance, or AMR, research programme, a long-running partnership between the two universities. Disarming Candida albicans Candida albicans normally lives harmlessly in the human body. However, in critically ill or immunocompromised patients, and particularly on medical devices such as catheters, the fungus can switch into an aggressive thread-like form known as hyphae. This form enables the fungus to penetrate tissue and form drug-resistant biofilms, which can lead to dangerous infections. The research team found that gladiolin does not prevent hyphae from forming in the first place. Instead, it accelerates the process by which Candida albicans reverts from the invasive hyphal form back to its harmless round yeast form once glucose becomes limited. By shortening the period in which the fungus remains invasive, gladiolin reduces the window in which it can cause damage. Professor Ana Traven, of the Monash Biomedicine Discovery Institute and co-lead of the Monash Warwick Alliance’s AMR programme, said the thread-like hyphae of Candida albicans allow the fungus to penetrate and damage human tissue and create drug-resistant biofilms. She said the team discovered that gladiolin effectively switches off this aggressive behaviour by pushing the fungus back into its less harmful state. Professor Traven said the findings offer a different way to think about controlling fungal infections, focused not only on killing the fungus but also on disarming it. Chemical trickery changes fungal metabolism The researchers found that gladiolin works through a form of chemical trickery. The molecule changes the fungus’s metabolism, causing Candida albicans to consume the glucose in its environment much faster than normal. Because hyphal growth depends on a steady supply of glucose, the fungus effectively runs out of the fuel it needs to remain in its invasive form. Dr Manasa Bharathwaj, first author of the study, said glucose is important for the growth of invasive hyphae. She said gladiolin tricks Candida into using up its glucose supply more quickly, forcing it to switch back to its less invasive yeast state. Building on earlier antifungal research The new study builds on a 2024 discovery from the same research team, which showed that gladiolin can also significantly increase the effectiveness of amphotericin B, one of the world’s most important antifungal drugs. Together, the studies suggest gladiolin may be able to combat fungal infections in two ways. It could help existing antifungal medicines work more effectively while also switching off the behaviour that makes the fungus dangerous. Professor Greg Challis, Monash Warwick Alliance Professor of Sustainable Chemistry at the University of Warwick and Monash University, said the findings suggest gladiolin could help existing drugs kill dangerous fungal pathogens, including drug-resistant biofilms that can form on medical devices. He added that the molecule may also allow lower and potentially less toxic doses of antifungal drugs to be used. Professor Challis said the work is an example of how interdisciplinary and international collaboration can open new approaches to antimicrobial resistance. Natural microbial warfare as a source of new treatments Gladiolin was discovered several years ago as a bacterial antibiotic, but its effects on fungal pathogens had not been fully understood. Professor Traven said microbes in nature compete for nutrients and space by producing molecules that are toxic to neighbouring microbes. She said these natural “microbial warfare” molecules can be used as inspiration for new medicines. Penicillin, she noted, is one of the best-known examples of this principle, as it is a molecule produced by a fungus to kill competing bacteria and later became one of the world’s most effective antibiotics. The team is applying a similar principle to gladiolin, exploring whether naturally occurring bacterial molecules can inspire new ways to treat deadly fungal infections. The findings contribute to the growing body of antimicrobial resistance research supported by the Monash Warwick Alliance’s strategic investment and grant funding schemes. title_en: Schools are starting to teach AI literacy. For many, that means helping kids see chatbots' flaws
summary: مدارس آمریکا به جای ممنوعیت مطلق، استراتژی آموزش «سواد هوش مصنوعی» و مواجهه مستقیم دانش‌آموزان با توهمات چت‌بات‌ها را در پیش گرفته‌اند.

full_text: Schools are starting to teach AI literacy. For many, that means helping kids see chatbots' flaws Artificial intelligence chatbots have become the bane of teachers everywhere, but to prepare for the new school year, a group of educators in Charleston, South Carolina, packed into a high school auditorium and talked about inviting AI into the classroom. The teachers and principals watched as an instructor prompted an AI tool to "create a map of the world." The result drew gasps of disbelief and laughter. Projected on a large screen was a map riddled with bizarre errors. Mali was spelled "Mail." Egypt was identified as "Sopth." In place of Libya was something simply called "Africa." Dozens of other countries' names were misspelled or written in pure gibberish. "If you ever want kids not to over trust these tools, try the map demo," said the instructor, Amanda Bickerstaff, founder and CEO of AI For Education, an organization that helps schools draft AI policies and train teachers and students in what she calls safe, ethical and effective use of the technology. After initially trying to ban AI use, a growing number of U.S. public schools are trying a new strategy: encouraging classroom experimentation, partly so students can see its shortcomings, including generative AI's notorious tendency to "hallucinate," or fabricate information. AI literacy has become a buzzword of this back-to-school season as educators try to strike a balance between equipping students with the skills they need for an AI-driven future while preventing them from outsourcing their thinking to chatbots. There is no single definition of what AI literacy means, or how it should be taught. Tech giants like OpenAI, Google and Anthropic offer schools training sessions in how to use their AI tools. But for educators, there is a growing consensus that AI literacy is about more than learning how to use generative AI and write good prompts. "Good AI literacy," said Rebecca Winthrop, director of the Center for Universal Education at the Brookings Institution, "includes knowing when not to use it." Some districts build their own approaches on AI literacy Thirty-seven states have now published official AI guidance that schools can use as a blueprint. South Carolina is not one of them. So the state's second-largest school district set out to do it on its own, said Lucas Clamp, deputy superintendent of the 50,000-student Charleston County School District. "It has been a huge endeavor." A year ago, the district contacted AI for Education, which helped draft guidance for Chicago Public Schools, Houston and dozens of other districts. Phase 1 was laying the foundation. The district developed an AI policy, seeking input from teachers, students and parents. The district organized student focus groups and learned that student AI use was ubiquitous but unguided. Teachers and students said they were navigating the technology on their own and wanted clear rules and instruction. Studies show a majority of teenagers and teachers nationwide are using AI for schoolwork, but they're teaching themselves how to use it; very few say they have a technical understanding or have received formal training on how it works. Schools and parents are eager to avoid mistakes made with social media, where kids were left to explore the online world without learning about addictive algorithms, comparison culture and other downsides that have been linked to a youth mental health crisis and dwindling attention spans. As the school year begins in Charleston, Phase 2 kicks in: training. Teachers and middle and high schoolers will get a mix of online and in-person instruction on how AI tools work and how to use them effectively. The student course walks through familiar scenarios—like asking a chatbot to help with a research paper—to show that generative AI might deliver wildly inaccurate information, including made-up studies, with unflinching authority. "Always verify any factual information you get from GenAI, especially for your classwork," the course advises. A section on data privacy cautions against sharing personal information with AI tools because conversations can be stored, used for data training and potentially leaked. High school teacher Ray Knauer attended the summer training and left with "teachable moments" for his AP Research class. He plans to show examples of AI bias and hallucinations to fuel student discussions. "We're all trying to figure this out right now: What's the right balance so we don't scare students away from AI but don't encourage them to run to it," Knauer said. "We have to teach students: You can't just get an answer and move on. You have to use analytical skills and dig deeper." Some states offer top-down guidance on AI in classrooms Utah was an early pioneer in taking a statewide approach to AI in education. In 2024, the board of education named Matt Winters as its AI education specialist, making Utah the first state to create a full-time position overseeing the technology in schools. Over the past year, Winters led AI training for over 7,000 teachers, almost a third of Utah's public school instructors. He is helping districts shape AI policies, which they are required by state law to have in place by July 2027. "There is a clear method from the top in Utah," said Chris Agnew, director of the Generative AI for Education Hub at Stanford University. "When you're tackling big change, it's easier to have coherence if everyone is singing from the same hymn book." A handful of other states have since replicated Winters' post, including Maine, West Virginia and Georgia. In other states, a patchwork of AI approaches has emerged, with variance from one school district to another. Extensive AI literacy training requires steep investment, raising concerns that kids in under-resourced districts might not get the same attention. title_fa: تراشه نوری جدید دانشمندان بریتانیا راه را برای ۶G هموار کرد
title_en: "Rainbow-on-a-chip" breakthrough could help unlock 6G networks and precision timing for quantum technologies
summary: فیزیکدانان دانشگاه لافبورو تراشه‌ای به اندازه یک دانه برنج ساخته‌اند که طیف‌های دقیق نوری تولید می‌کند.
ترکیب تشدیدکننده روی تراشه با فیبر نوری، پایداری بی‌سابقه‌ای برای تولید امواج میلی‌متری شبکه ۶G فراهم کرده است.
این دستاورد علاوه بر مخابرات، کاربردهای گسترده‌ای در رادارهای پیشرفته و محاسبات کوانتومی دارد.
full_text: Loughborough University physicists and an international team have demonstrated that a grain-of-rice-sized microchip can be used to produce a spectrum of precisely spaced frequencies of light, which is then converted into multiple high-frequency electromagnetic signals known as millimetre waves. Millimetre waves are of growing interest for future communications because they offer much more bandwidth – essentially more space for transmitting data – but generating them with precision and stability needed for advanced technologies remains challenging. “The world is becoming increasingly data hungry. We want to send and receive more information, faster and in higher resolution, and millimetre waves could help provide the capacity to do that,” said Dr Luke Peters, of Loughborough University’s Emergent Photonics Research Centre. “They could ultimately contribute to faster, higher capacity 6G networks, but the potential goes far beyond communications. These frequencies could also be used in radar systems as well as spectroscopy and astronomical instruments, helping scientists study materials and make extremely precise measurements of the universe. “These applications are still some way off, and there are challenges to overcome before the technology can be used in real-world systems – but our latest work has tackled a major one.” One way to generate millimetre waves is using a microcomb – a highly precise spectrum of light frequencies, arranged similar to the colours of a rainbow but invisible to the human eye. These light frequencies can be converted into millimetre waves using a specialised antenna. In a new Nature Communications paper, the Loughborough-led team has demonstrated just that. They have created a system that produces a stable, high-quality microcomb that can be converted into multiple precisely spaced millimetre-wave frequencies at once. The key is the way the team generates its microcomb. Microcombs are typically created by shining laser light into a microresonator – a tiny structure on a microchip that traps and circulates light. The Loughborough design works differently by combining the chip-based microresonator with a larger loop of optical fibre, creating a system in which the laser light continually circulates through both. The ‘rainbow on a chip’: a tiny microchip containing a microresonator that produces a precisely organised ‘rainbow’ of light frequencies, known as a microcomb. The chip is the size of a grain of rice, with a one euro coin pictured for scale. “We’ve essentially created an incredibly precise and stable ‘rainbow on a chip’, where the loop keeps feeding the light back through the chip, allowing these states to build up efficiently, start on their own and remain stable even when the system is disturbed”, said Dr Peters. “It’s remarkably robust too. We’ve even had people jumping up and down next to the system and the microcomb remains stable.” Researchers from the Emergent Photonics Research Centre put their microcomb system’s stability to the test by jumping next to it. In their latest study, the team also demonstrated that they could control the microcomb “rainbow”, making some frequencies stronger or weaker. Crucially, they showed that its precision and stability was carried through to the millimetre-wave signals it produced. “Being able to make individual frequencies stronger or weaker gives us much more control over the signals we produce, because different applications will need different combinations of frequencies,” said Dr Peters. “Just as importantly, we’ve shown that the precision of the microcomb carries through to the millimetre waves. That gives us a whole set of highly controlled signals, which is exactly what you need for applications where accuracy and stability matter. “That same level of precision is valuable for timing. Precision timing sits at the core of emerging quantum technologies, where extreme accuracy is a requirement.” What’s next The researchers are now exploring how their microcomb technology could be taken beyond the laboratory. While the microchip at its heart is the size of a grain of rice, the complete system is currently a tabletop laboratory set-up. Future versions could be even more compact and energy efficient – potentially small enough to fit inside a shoebox. The team is particularly interested in exploring whether the technology could one day be used on satellites, where size, weight and power are important. Precision timing for quantum technologies The researchers are also exploring just how accurate their microcomb set-up could be. The team is testing it against precision clocks and exploring potential applications in timing, navigation and position through collaborations with the National Physical Laboratory and is an integral part of the efforts of the National Physical Laboratory and the UK Hub for Quantum Enabled Position, Navigation and Timing (QEPNT). “We’re really excited to see how far we can take the precision and stability of these microcombs, particularly for technologies that rely on extremely accurate timing,” said Dr Antonio Cutrona, who led the microcomb stability measurements. “We hope this study and our system open up new ways of bringing the extraordinary precision of atomic clocks into more compact technologies for timing, navigation and position, and it is particularly exciting to explore these possibilities through our wider collaborations with the National Physical Laboratory and the UK Hub for Quantum Enabled Position, Navigation and Timing.” The study brings together expertise from Loughborough University’s Emergent Photonics Research Centre, the University of Sussex, City University of Hong Kong, QXP Technologies, INRS-EMT, and Swinburne University of Technology and ARC-COMBS.

impact: حل چالش پایداری فرکانسی، ساخت زیرساخت‌های واقعی اینترنت ۶G و ابزارهای سنجش کوانتومی را تسریع می‌کند.

full_text: A few years ago, I wrote a memorable and quite controversial story about Jeanne Calment, who was then – and remains now – the official holder of the world longevity record. She was born in 1875 and died in 1997, aged 122 years and 164 days. At least that’s the official version of events. According to some doubters, the woman who died as Jeanne Calment was actually her daughter Yvonne, who fraudulently assumed her mother’s identity when Jeanne died in 1934. Yvonne was 23 years Jeanne’s junior. Still a good innings, but not a record-breaking one. The matter remains unresolved, and so, for now, Calment remains one of the most important data points in biogerontology. When we ask, “how long can a person live?”, the answer is “at least 122 years and 164 days” – assuming Jeanne Calment really did live that long. Whether a person could live longer has long troubled scientists. It’s an important question in biogerontology because, if we want to achieve life extension, we need to know what we’re aiming for. But it’s surprisingly hard to answer. Calment is an outlier: nobody else has reached 120, which is one reason for the suspicion. The second-longest-lived person was Kane Tanaka, who racked up 119 years and 107 days, and the oldest person today has just turned 117. Aside from a few mavericks, however, everyone agrees that there is a natural limit. Advertisement But where is it? There are two main ways of tackling this question. One is by studying demographic data on verified supercentenarians. One such frequently cited analysis produced an estimate of roughly 115, but did not rule out somebody living to 125. Another concluded that Calment’s record is likely to be broken fairly soon. Another approach is by computer modelling. One such model analysed short-term fluctuations in red and white blood cell counts in adults aged 85 and over, which the researchers converted into a measure of their resilience to terminal age-related disease. At some point, resilience breaks down completely, marking the point of no return. The researchers concluded that this varies from person to person, usually kicking in at about 120. But even for the most resilient individuals there is a hard upper limit of 150. There’s a big difference between 125 and 150, and we’ll get onto this. But one thing these studies don’t take into account is future advances in medicine. In the 1920s, scientists believed that it was impossible to live past 105, according to biogerontologist Richard Faragher at the University of Brighton, UK. But over the following century, medical breakthroughs steadily added years to people’s life expectancies, helping (along with better nutrition and sanitation) to nudge the longevity record upwards. What happens if that trend continues? To find out, a team at the Skolkovo Institute of Science and Technology and the Artificial Intelligence Research Institute, both in Moscow, Russia, ran a thought experiment. Imagine, they said, that we manage to cure all the theoretically curable causes of ageing. The only unfixable one is damage to the DNA in our cells, which accumulates remorselessly as we age. In that scenario, the upper limit of a human life soars to 194 years. I’ll stick my neck out and say it ain’t going to happen in my lifetime, and also point out that the causes of ageing are not yet fully understood. Even so, it suggests there’s quite a lot of room for improvement. But back to the real world. Why do upper age estimates vary so much? Re-enter Jeanne Calment. When I was reporting that story, I spoke to a longevity researcher called Saul Newman, then at the Australian National University in Canberra. He had just published a paper showing that a small number of errors or fraudulent entries in paper records such as birth certificates can significantly distort longevity data. He told me he suspected the Calments’ alleged identity fraud was just the tip of the iceberg. Newman, now at the University of Oxford, has just published a book, Morbid: Debunking modern longevity science, revealing the shocking extent of those errors and frauds. In Greece, for example, around 70 per cent of centenarians were found to be dead, kept alive on paper so their relatives could keep on drawing their pensions. Even higher levels of pension fraud were discovered in Japan. People have historically inflated their age for many other reasons, to join (or dodge) military service, get married or get a job. Clerical errors are rife too, especially from the time when today’s centenarians and supercentenarians were born. These errors inevitably feed into estimates of the upper limit of human longevity. If the demographic data used as an input is riddled with inflated ages, the output is probably also inflated. Garbage in, garbage out. People used in modelling studies are also tagged with an age, which could well be wrong. When the journal Nature asked Newman where this leaves the debate about a maximum human lifespan, he answered: “in an absolute shambles.” When I was researching the Calment story, I also came across a 2011 paper that found that, across the whole world, 98 per cent of claims of lifespans over 115 could not be verified. The same paper also found that, in countries with rigorous birth records going back more than 150 years, not one person has been proved to have lived past 115. That, I think, is the best estimate we’ve got. Five score years and fifteen. I’m halfway there.

full_text: (Bloomberg) -- Nvidia Corp. is in early discussions with the Korean AI chip designer Rebellions about possible collaborations, including a technical partnership, an investment or perhaps even an acquisition, according to people familiar with the matter. Most Read from Bloomberg Nvidia Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang met with Rebellions co-founder and CEO Sunghyun Park and discussed a potential tie-up at the US company's headquarters in Santa Clara, California this week, said the people, who asked not to be identified as the information is not public. Huang has led a far-reaching investment spree in recent years, as Nvidia works to maintain its central role in the artificial intelligence era. Those deals have included high-profile startups. In late 2025, Nvidia struck an unconventional deal with US AI firm Groq, securing a nonexclusive license while absorbing most of its engineering talent. Nvidia said it wasn't an acquisition because Groq continues to operate separately and run its cloud business independently. Bundang, South Korea-based Rebellions has raised roughly $850 million from investors including SK Hynix Inc., Samsung Ventures and Arm Holdings Plc, and was most recently valued at around $2.3 billion. It has also secured a direct investment from the Korean government. Deliberations between Nvidia and six-year-old Rebellions are preliminary and may not lead to a transaction, the people said. Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment. A representative for Rebellions declined to comment. Founded in the midst of the pandemic in 2020, Rebellions is among a group of semiconductor startups designing and deploying their own chips to rival market leader Nvidia. The company specializes in neural processing units for data centers, optimized for AI inference work. Less intensive in processing requirements than AI training, inference is the larger-in-volume workload required to operate AI services at scale. Nvidia holds such a dominant share of the semiconductors used to train AI models like those from OpenAI and Anthropic PBC that it has to be wary of antitrust scrutiny. Large acquisitions in the tech industry typically need clearance from authorities such as the US Department of Justice.

full_text: TL;DR - NVIDIA will provide over $105 billion in financing for OpenAI's Ohio data center campus - The PORTS-Pike facility could house 1.5 million NVIDIA GPUs across 8 gigawatts of capacity - SB Energy will build and own the site; OpenAI leases it for 20 years - NVIDIA made a separate $1.5 billion equity investment in SB Energy - Jensen Huang explicitly denied this constitutes circular investing in a blog post NVIDIA isn’t just selling chips to the AI industry anymore — it’s financing the buildings they go in. The company announced Monday that it will provide more than $105 billion to secure land, power, and shell construction for OpenAI’s planned Ohio data center campus, marking one of the largest infrastructure financing commitments in technology history. Inside the PORTS-Pike Technology Campus Deal The three-way arrangement between NVIDIA, OpenAI, and SB Energy reveals how AI infrastructure deals are structured in 2026. SB Energy will ultimately build and own the facility, known as the PORTS-Pike Technology Campus. OpenAI will lease the site for 20 years. NVIDIA’s role is financing the physical prerequisites — land acquisition, power procurement, and building shells — that make construction possible. Initial plans call for 4.25 gigawatts of computing capacity, with options to scale to 8 gigawatts total. To put that in perspective, 8 gigawatts exceeds the electrical output of most nuclear power plants. NVIDIA estimates the site could house roughly 1.5 million GPUs, translating to potential revenue of $150 billion to $200 billion per generation deployed through 2030. NVIDIA also made a separate $1.5 billion equity investment in SB Energy as part of the arrangement. Combined with prior agreements between NVIDIA and OpenAI, the total deal value could reach as much as $600 billion. Jensen Huang Says This Isn’t Circular Investing The elephant in the room is obvious: NVIDIA invests in the infrastructure, which then buys NVIDIA’s chips. That pattern — investing in a customer who turns around and spends the money on your products — is textbook circular investing, a practice that raises red flags about inflated revenue figures. Huang addressed this directly in a blog post published Monday, writing that NVIDIA “uses its scale and long-term visibility to secure PORTS-Pike to host NVIDIA compute.” He compared the approach to supply-chain management, where companies secure critical inputs when they have clear visibility into customer demand. “This is the same discipline we apply to supply-chain management: we secure critical inputs when we have visibility into customer demand and when doing so enables long-term productive capacity,” Huang wrote. He also clarified that NVIDIA will only cover portions of lease and power payments — not the full cost of the site or OpenAI’s operational obligations. We think the distinction matters but won’t satisfy every skeptic. NVIDIA isn’t handing cash to OpenAI to buy GPUs. Instead, it’s financing the physical infrastructure that makes GPU deployment possible. The chips themselves are a separate transaction. However, the practical effect remains: NVIDIA’s investment reduces the barriers for OpenAI to buy more NVIDIA hardware. Whether you call that strategic supply-chain management or financial engineering depends on your viewpoint. NVIDIA’s Dealmaking Machine Won’t Stop This Ohio campus deal landed just days after NVIDIA announced a separate $500 billion fund with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs, and KKR to finance AI data center construction globally. The company has also invested in Ilya Sutskever’s Safe Superintelligence startup and SK Hynix, the memory chip manufacturer critical to GPU production. The pattern is clear. NVIDIA is building an ecosystem where every layer of the AI infrastructure stack — from memory chips to data center financing to the physical buildings themselves — has NVIDIA’s fingerprints on it. When Jensen Huang talks about “securing the infrastructure of intelligence,” he means NVIDIA wants to be the landlord, the builder, and the equipment supplier simultaneously. We’ve noticed this strategy accelerating throughout 2026. Each new deal makes the next one easier because NVIDIA can point to its growing infrastructure portfolio as proof of committed demand. It’s a flywheel effect: more infrastructure partnerships generate more GPU orders, which generate more revenue, which funds more infrastructure partnerships. What This Means for the AI Industry The PORTS-Pike campus represents a broader shift in how AI infrastructure gets built and financed. Traditionally, cloud providers like Microsoft, Amazon, and Google funded their own data centers. OpenAI’s arrangement — leasing a facility backed by its chip supplier — creates a new model where hardware companies become infrastructure financiers. This matters because it addresses the single biggest constraint on AI scaling: the speed at which data centers can be built and powered. By financing land and power procurement upfront, NVIDIA removes months or years of lead time from the development process. For OpenAI, it also represents a step toward controlling its own infrastructure rather than relying entirely on cloud provider capacity. The risk for NVIDIA is concentration. A significant portion of its revenue growth thesis now depends on a small number of massive data center projects reaching completion and operational status. If power availability, permitting, or construction delays slow the PORTS-Pike timeline, the GPU orders associated with the facility get pushed back too.
